title: Converts and reverts
hookLine: people who come to Islam, called reverts by some, who often face welcome and challenges

lines: A DATE, ALONE AT THE COUNTER.
cards: Her first Ramadan, she breaks the fast alone at her kitchen counter with a date and a glass of water, because her family doesn't fast and she doesn't know anyone at the mosque yet.

Her second Ramadan, somebody she met at Friday prayer texts her an address and the words: come, we'll save you a seat. Same woman, same faith, same dates on the plate. What changed was one text message.
Some people who come to Islam as adults tell stories like hers. Some call themselves converts. Some call themselves reverts.

teach.h: REVERT: A RETURN TO THE FITRA.
teach.b: Back on day one hundred fifty-one, i said everyone started new. Today, a closer look. Some new Muslims prefer revert, and explain it from a hadith in al-Bukhari.
In paraphrase: every child is born upon the fitra, the natural disposition, and it is the parents who shape the child into one way or another.
If every person begins on that disposition, coming to Islam is a return, not a switch. Others are happy with convert, or new Muslim. The kindest move: ask which word they use.
The door is a sentence. A person becomes Muslim by bearing witness, the shahada: there is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah. No class must be finished first.
And the Qur'an insists the choice is free, in Pickthall's words: "There is no compulsion in religion."
Nobody here starts as an insider. In the first generation, no one had been raised Muslim. Khadijah.
Abu Bakr. Bilal, who had been enslaved. Tradition tells of Salman the Persian, who searched through teacher after teacher and land after land before reaching Madinah.
Welcome and challenge are both real. Surah al-Tawbah names among those who may receive zakat the ones whose hearts are to be brought close, and scholars have included new Muslims among them.
Some mosques run circles for new Muslims and invite them to iftars.

And new Muslims describe the hard parts: a family that doesn't understand, learning the prayers in Arabic, not knowing which customs are faith and which are culture, and the loneliness of an Eid with nowhere to go.

how: A person becomes Muslim by bearing witness, the shahada, that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His messenger; some mosques welcome new Muslims with study circles, mentors and invitations to iftar, and some communities ask which word, convert or revert, a person prefers.

games.q: a coworker tells you she became Muslim last year. you're not sure whether to say convert or revert. what do you do?
o: pick one and correct her if she uses the other.
ask her which word she uses.
games.why: both words are in use, and people hold them for real reasons; asking is the simple, kind move.

practice: Remember a time you were the new one, at a school, a job, a city, a dinner where you knew nobody, and the person who made it a little easier. What did they actually do: remember your name, save you a seat, ask you a question?
Hold that small act for a few breaths, and if you pray, thank Allah for that person in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Converts and reverts. People who come to Islam as adults; some say revert, as a return to the fitra, some say convert. Ask which word they use. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the natural disposition every child is born upon, in the hadith; the reason some new Muslims say revert.

carryVoice: Your line: new to it. A saved seat can change a whole Ramadan. Back tomorrow, same hill.
